entities.name: William the Hardy, Lord of Douglas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sir William Douglas "le Hardi", Lord of Douglas (died 1298), stands as a pivotal early figure in the Scottish Wars of Independence, whose defiance against Edward I of England solidified the nascent spirit of resistance among the Scottish nobility. As the first recorded Lord of Douglas, he established the formidable reputation of one of Scotland's most powerful and enduring aristocratic families. His actions, marked by shifting allegiances and steadfast opposition to English annexation, placed him at the heart of the tumultuous Anglo-Scottish relations in the late 13th century, directly influencing the political landscape that would give rise to national heroes like William Wallace and Robert the Bruce.

Douglas's active resistance commenced dramatically in 1296 when, following Edward I's invasion of Scotland, he famously captured Berwick Castle from the English, an act of overt rebellion against the English crown which had by then claimed suzerainty over Scotland. His subsequent oath of fealty to Edward I, known as the Ragman Roll, proved short-lived, as he swiftly joined William Wallace's insurgency. This renewed defiance led to his capture by English forces at the Capitulation of Irvine in 1297, alongside other Scottish nobles. Despite further oaths and paroles, his consistent refusal to submit fully to English rule defined his public life and military career.

His ultimate fate, death in the Tower of London in 1298, transformed him into an early martyr for Scottish independence, a symbol of unyielding national spirit. William the Hardy's legacy was profoundly carried forward by his son, James Douglas, known as "the Black Douglas," who became one of Robert the Bruce's most trusted and formidable commanders. The Douglas clan, forged in the fires of these wars, would become synonymous with Scottish martial prowess and a dominant force in the nation's history for centuries, directly owing their initial prominence to the defiant stand of their progenitor.
